query: For boride-based components used in hot-dip aluminum-plating equipment, what single intervention could improve resistance to molten-aluminum corrosion? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts the improvement relative to an appropriate baseline, defines the conditions under which it should remain effective, cites supporting prior evidence, and specifies a controlled experiment whose results could falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: A controlled thermal pre-oxidation treatment to form a continuous, adherent Al₂O₃ surface scale on the boride-based component will significantly enhance its resistance to molten-aluminum corrosion.
generation.material_initial_state: Boride-based components with standard microstructure as used in hot-dip aluminum-plating equipment.
generation.intervention: Expose the component to a controlled high-temperature oxidizing environment prior to aluminum plating to promote formation of a thin, dense alumina (Al₂O₃) layer.
generation.conditions: Temperatures sufficient to promote Al₂O₃ formation (e.g., 700–900 °C) in an oxygen-containing atmosphere for an optimized time, followed by a controlled cooling cycle; the treatment should be compatible with current manufacturing practices.
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of an adherent, continuous Al₂O₃ barrier layer on the surface.
generation.mechanism: The pre-formed alumina layer acts as an inert diffusion barrier that impedes direct contact between molten aluminum and the underlying boride substrate, thereby reducing the rate of interfacial chemical attack and limiting aluminum dissolution processes.
generation.predicted_outcome: A measurable reduction in the corrosion rate of the treated component relative to untreated boride surfaces, with potentially a substantial (>20%) improvement in service lifetime under molten-aluminum exposure.
generation.baseline: Standard boride components without any pre-oxidation treatment that develop a less protective or discontinuous oxide during service.
generation.boundary: Effectiveness is expected to sustain under typical hot-dip conditions; however, if the thermal pre-oxidation process leads to spallation or if the oxide layer is too thick (leading to cracking), the beneficial effect may be compromised.
generation.uncertainty: The optimal temperature, time, and cooling rate for generating a defect-free alumina layer specific to these boride components require further investigation.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of boride-based specimens; subject one set to a controlled thermal pre-oxidation treatment and leave the other untreated. Expose both sets to molten aluminum under identical plating conditions.
measurements: Oxide layer thickness and integrity (via SEM/XRD)
Corrosion rate measurements (mass loss, electrochemical tests)
Surface morphology and composition after exposure
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the pre-oxidized samples do not exhibit a statistically significant lower corrosion rate or improved oxide integrity compared to the untreated baseline under molten aluminum conditions, the hypothesis would be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: The oxide scale morphologies of the coatings are shown in Figure 10c,g and the EDS analysis is shown in Table 4. It can be concluded that the oxidation corrosion products of the coatings were mainly Al-rich oxides. Additionally, there was also a certain amount of FeCr-rich oxides. Combined with the XRD results in Figure 9, it can be concluded that the corrosion product was mainly Al2O3. By analyzing the morphology and EDS of the corroded areas, it can be concluded that the elemental depletion of the EHEA coating was faster than that of the YHf coating, and trace amounts of sulfur elements were detected in the corroded areas of the EHEA. In conclusion, all coatings exhibited the same corrosion mechanism. The YHf-EHEA coating showed better resistance to the 75% Na2SO4 + 25% NaCl molten salts hot corrosion than the EHEA coating at 900 °C. The mechanism for the coatings under Na2SO4 + NaCl hot corrosion is described as follows [,,,]. Initially, chlorine reacts with the metal to form metal chlorides (MClx). However, at a temperature of 900 °C, the metal oxides (MxOy) have a lower Gibbs formation free energy than the metal chlorides, leading to the transformation of the metal chlorides i

Corrosion resistance of alloys in light water reactors (LWRs) and more generally in oxidative environments is achieved by the formation of protective oxide layers that hinder further oxidation. Alloys containing Cr, Al, or Si typically tend to form a compact and self-healing chromia (Cr2O3), alumina (Al2O3) or silica (SiO2) layers, respectively, which acts as effective diffusion barriers against further oxidation. However, in molten fluoride salts (salt of choice for many molten salt reactor concepts, MSRs) these protective oxide layers on structural alloys are unstable which in turn leads to the dissolution of the least noble element in the alloy. Such a corrosion mechanism can lead to a reduction in components’ wall thickness and eventually the loss of the structural integrity of the reactor components,. The dissolution products themselves may lead to plate-out in the relatively cooler sections of the system due to the strong sensitivity of solubility of analytes to temperature.
